title: Checkpoint: The First Great Stories
objective: After this level you can explain what myths are and how the oldest stories were composed, written down and passed on.
summary: Ashurbanipal's scribes copied old texts at Nineveh. When it fell in 612 BCE, the ruins buried the clay tablets until the 1800s. Stories survive by memory, copying and luck.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 finale: how did stories this old reach you at all?
cards.body: Every story in this chapter nearly vanished. Here they are in order, then the luckiest escape of all, then the three ways a story survives.

cards.headline: The first great stories reach the page

events.label: Sumerian poems of Gilgamesh on clay tablets
Homer's epics take shape among singers
Ashurbanipal's scribes copy old texts at Nineveh
The Kojiki is written down from memory

cards.headline: A fallen city kept the king's library
cards.body: The Assyrian king Ashurbanipal had his scribes collect and copy ancient texts of every kind, from prayers to fables and epics. In 612 BCE an alliance including Babylonians and Medes sacked his capital, Nineveh, and the ruined walls buried the clay tablets. From 1845, Austen Henry Layard and then Hormuzd Rassam dug them out, and more than 20,000 tablets and fragments went to the British Museum. Among them: the 12 tablets of Gilgamesh.

cards.headline: Memory, copying, luck
cards.body: Look back at how this chapter's stories survived. Memory: Homer's singers inherited phrases, scenes and plots, and the Kojiki began in Hieda no Are's memory. Copying: Ashurbanipal's scribes. Luck: a sacked city that buried its library, and a self-taught engraver who spotted a ship on a mountain and a dove on a broken tablet.

mascot.line: Don't memorize every date. Remember the three ways a story survives: memory, copying and luck.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete

questions.prompt: How did the clay tablets of Ashurbanipal's library survive the fall of Nineveh?

options.label: Scribes carried them safely to Babylon
They were copied onto paper in time
Monks hid them in a mountain cave
options.rationale: They were buried in the ruins.

questions.explanation: When Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE, the ruined walls buried the tablets until excavators dug them out in the 1800s.

questions.prompt: Why could George Smith read a Babylonian flood story in London in 1872?

options.label: Excavators had taken Nineveh's tablets to the British Museum
The story had always been printed in English Bibles
options.rationale: It was lost until he read it.

options.label: A Babylonian scribe had mailed a copy
options.rationale: The tablets were dug from Nineveh's ruins.

options.label: Homer had translated it into Greek
options.rationale: Homer's epics are a separate tradition.

questions.explanation: Layard and Rassam dug the Nineveh tablets out, and more than 20,000 went to the British Museum, where Smith worked.

questions.prompt: Chapter recap: which of these was written down first?

options.label: Ashurbanipal's copies at Nineveh
options.rationale: Those copied older texts in the 7th century BCE.

questions.explanation: Sumerian poems about Gilgamesh survive on tablets from the early 2nd millennium BCE, long before the others.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: a traditional story told as history, about a particular person or place, is called what?

options.label: A myth
options.rationale: A myth is tied to religious belief.

options.label: A fable
options.rationale: A fable has animals and a moral.

options.label: A folk tale
options.rationale: A folk tale is told for the tale itself.

questions.explanation: A legend is told as a matter of history, like William Tell and the apple, whether or not it happened.

questions.prompt: From Level 5: in the Haudenosaunee creation story, what does the muskrat bring up from the water?

options.label: A little earth that grows on a turtle's back
A plant that renews youth, stolen by a snake

questions.explanation: The muskrat brings up a little earth, and on the turtle's back it grows into North America, Turtle Island.
